answers.answer:
In SCOP 1.75, 1acc chain A (anthrax protective antigen, PA; UniProt P13423; 735 residues in the SEQRES) was a single whole-chain domain, d1acca_ (sunid 43828, f.11.1.1, 'A:'). That placed it in class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides), as a pore-forming toxin. In SCOPe 2.08 the same chain is split into two domains. d1acca2 (sunid 238522) covers A:14-225 and is b.179.1.1: class b (all beta), fold b.179 (anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like), superfamily b.179.1 (PA14-like), family PA14. d1acca1 (sunid 238521) covers A:226-735 and is f.60.1.1: class f, fold, superfamily and family all named 'Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like'. So one chain-level assignment became two domains with different classes, folds, superfamilies and families. I did not retrieve the intermediate releases (such as 2.01-2.07), so I can't say in which release the split first appeared. I also did not check whether other regions are unassigned, and the 1.75 'A:' range was not itemized.

What this shows about domains as evolutionary modules: a single polypeptide can be a fusion of independently evolving units. Each unit can have its own fold, its own homologs and its own evolutionary history. The N-terminal PA14 module is a beta module that also occurs in other proteins, such as glycosidases and adhesins. The C-terminal region is a distinct pore-forming and receptor-binding architecture. Chain-level classification fuses these histories, and it is only a proxy that happened to work when the structural domain boundaries were not yet recognized. A SCOP domain is a unit of homology and structure, not a unit of gene, chain or function. Revised domain boundaries are therefore expected as the PDB grows and as new relatives of each module reveal where the evolutionary units are.

Implications for homology searches: (1) Search with domain-level queries, not the whole chain. A whole-chain query or a legacy chain-level label mixes signals from two unrelated modules. Hits to the PA14 module say nothing about the C-terminal region, and the reverse is also true. (2) Take the domain-level lineage from the current release, such as d1acca2 or d1acca1 in 2.08, not from 1.75 d1acca_ or its f.11.1.1 label. Old sids and sunids can be obsolete or mapped differently, so pin the release in any comparison. (3) A hit covering only part of a chain supports homology only for the aligned module. Do not transfer the other domain's fold, superfamily or function, and do not transfer an official classification to a target from a reference lineage. That is candidate evidence only. (4) Shared fold or class alone is not homology; in SCOPe, homology is asserted at the superfamily and family levels. The two domains here are in different classes, so they are not related by a SCOPe homology claim, even though they sit in the same chain. (5) Domain count, boundaries and function should come from evidence per region. Multidomain proteins need per-region hit coverage, and benchmarks and templates should not be built from stale single-domain assignments, or from a representative chain whose domains were split differently. The cluster representative for 1accA is 3tewA, with 96.9% identity, and I did not use it for classification.

In SCOPe 2.08 the same chain is split into two domains. d1acca2 (sunid 238522) covers A:14-225 and is b.179.1.1: class b (all beta), fold b.179 (anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like), superfamily b.179.1 (PA14-like), family PA14. d1acca1 (sunid 238521) covers A:226-735 and is f.60.1.1: class f, fold, superfamily and family all named 'Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like'. So one chain-level assignment became two domains with different classes, folds, superfamilies and families. I did not retrieve the intermediate releases (such as 2.01-2.07), so I can't say in which release the split first appeared. I also did not check whether other regions are unassigned, and the 1.75 'A:' range was not itemized.

What this shows about domains as evolutionary modules: a single polypeptide can be a fusion of independently evolving units. Each unit can have its own fold, its own homologs and its own evolutionary history. The N-terminal PA14 module is a beta module that also occurs in other proteins, such as glycosidases and adhesins. The C-terminal region is a distinct pore-forming and receptor-binding architecture. Chain-level classification fuses these histories, and it is only a proxy that happened to work when the structural domain boundaries were not yet recognized. A SCOP domain is a unit of homology and structure, not a unit of gene, chain or function. Revised domain boundaries are therefore expected as the PDB grows and as new relatives of each module reveal where the evolutionary units are.

Implications for homology searches: (1) Search with domain-level queries, not the whole chain. A whole-chain query or a legacy chain-level label mixes signals from two unrelated modules. Hits to the PA14 module say nothing about the C-terminal region, and the reverse is also true. (2) Take the domain-level lineage from the current release, such as d1acca2 or d1acca1 in 2.08, not from 1.75 d1acca_ or its f.11.1.1 label. Old sids and sunids can be obsolete or mapped differently, so pin the release in any comparison. (3) A hit covering only part of a chain supports homology only for the aligned module. Do not transfer the other domain's fold, superfamily or function, and do not transfer an official classification to a target from a reference lineage. That is candidate evidence only. (4) Shared fold or class alone is not homology; in SCOPe, homology is asserted at the superfamily and family levels. The two domains here are in different classes, so they are not related by a SCOPe homology claim, even though they sit in the same chain. (5) Domain count, boundaries and function should come from evidence per region. Multidomain proteins need per-region hit coverage, and benchmarks and templates should not be built from stale single-domain assignments, or from a representative chain whose domains were split differently. The cluster representative for 1accA is 3tewA, with 96.9% identity, and I did not use it for classification.
